## 2. Portrayals of grief

**Score:** 25
**Body:** Heyy y'all! Would you pls recommend me a movie/series that portrays grief and genuinely touched your soul? Regardless of its nationality, length,...

Feel free to talk about it more if you want, I'd love to hear what made it so meaningful to you

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Manchester By The Sea is a film that shows how differently grief can impact people 
  - I was gonna say this! The whole movie is a portrayal of grief. 
2. I really liked The Descendants (2011) .  
3. Reign Over Me - It made me meaningful because I'm used to see Adam Sandler happy and somewhat funny, and suddenly it's a different side. It reminds me how inreal life when you see someone being happy from the outside, and different on the inside. 

What Dreams May Come - Because, well, Robin Williams is amazing in these kind of stuff.

5. The Way, dir. Emilio Estevez. A father (Martin Sheen) walks the Camino in honour if his late son (played by Emilio Estevez, making it even more poignant.
)

I cried like a baby watching it. A very moving, sincere film.

7. Babadook

Dear Zachary

Season 1 of Them
8. Six feet under
9. Midsommar 

## 3. Movies about moving on after loved ones suicide

**Score:** 23
**Body:** 2 days ago I was heading home from a friend's get together, and my partner told me our friend intentionally overdosed that morning. I've been feeling so lost since then. We weren't incredibly close, but we had a strong connection over being disabled and losing our hopes and dreams. I feel like I should've been there for her, I should've called her more, invited her out, done SOMETHING more. And I also feel angry at her; how could she leave our friends, her wife, her toddler, her… disabled friend who felt seen for once. I can't bring myself to talk about it to anyone yet, whenever I try the most I can muster is "I'm good." 

Sorry for rambling, my brain feels like I'm stuck in a fog of mixed feelings that I can't identify or make sense of. I need to see someone else navigate these feelings. Especially the hurt, guilt, confusion, anger, selfishness, and something I can't even begin to explain. I just need some catharsis right now 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. manchester by the sea came to mind. it handles grief, guilt, and anger in a way that felt very real to me.
  - I've been thinking a lot about that one since it happened. I need to work my way up to it though, I don't think I'm ready to watch this movie again yet. Hell, I didn't feel ready to rewatch it yet before I got the news tbh
2. The Big Chill.  I watched it the day after a close friends funeral and it was very meaningful.
  - Such a good movie with an excellent soundtrack.
3. Ordinary People
4. Aftersun
5. Not exactly what you’re looking for but The Fisher King deals with similar topics 
6. Harold and Maude
7. Non suicide but absolutely the most soulful life-opening movie is Margaret. Just how it deals with grief and feeling responsible for something terrible happening and avoiding pain and how that all can just leak into your life unless you deal with it…..it’s just a great movie. 


8. Not a movie but Fleabag came to mind first. I've lost too many friends to suicide, it is the worst.

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. So I watched Backrooms for the first time today. I found it very underwhelming.

**Score:** 727
**Body:** So the movie starts off with Mary and Clark doing some kind of therapy and the exploration  the psychological aspect was good but poor in execution . 

But then, it later turns into some kind of monster chase movie. Then abrupt ending showing rooms and distorted figures. There’s no clear resolution to what happens to Mary after she gets interrogated by the scientists.

Not only that, Clark doesn’t seem to grow as a character at all. Like, the film explains him getting kicked out of his wife due to some marital issues, but what does he learn from it? 

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think Clark not growing was part of the point of the movie.  He blames everyone else for every issue in his life.  He blames his wife for him not having his dream job.  For being stuck selling shitty furniture.  For him being an alcoholic.

Mary was focusing on this aspect during therapy.  Trying to get him to stop blaming others and to take some responsibility for his own actions.

After his time in the Backrooms, he seems to be introspective.  But then he has that last minute roleplaying with Mary where he wants her to tell him he doesn't need to change, doesn't need to grow.  When "twisted Clark" shows up, you can tell Clark has had interactions with him in the past.  Then, in that last encounter, he says "She says we don't need to change!" at which point Clark is killed by his own mental projection.

Mary, on the other hand, does grow and change.  She has fought through a much worse mental situation than Clark has.  But she's been hanging on to that past trauma.  She's carrying around the handprint, which I think represents being haunted by her past.  When she's in dire trouble, she uses that handprint and shatters it, allowing her to eventually escape from the Backrooms.

Maybe I'm reading too much into the movie, giving it depth that isn't there.  The whole thing seems like an allegory for mental health to me.  The Backrooms representing our own internal memories, our internal monsters, how our brains twist our memories.  Delving into the Backrooms representing delving into our own pasts, our memories and our traumas.  Mary and Clark are the two different paths we can take.  Either making an effort to grow and move on, or getting stuck in our same patterns and refusing to change.
  - I think this is a pretty good analysis. 
  - A very interesting idea is that Captain Clark isn’t a projection of Clark’s, it’s a misremembered version left behind by his ex-wife. Which makes why that version of her panics and hides even more interesting. 

I really enjoyed the ambiguity. I know audience expect explanations. But I really loved that it didn’t. Even by the end, the “expert” had no idea. It’s just this anomaly that makes no sense. 

And by the end that last sequence of images, misremembered versions of Mary’s past. Her sat in that chair without any explanation, like a part of her will forever be there wondering where she is. But like Clark said, there, she’s remembered. 

Just a really unsettling idea. Those are my favourite kind of horror films, because you’re just left with the haunt of it in your imagination. 
2. I loved it and was pleasantly surprised by its weirdness. 
3. I mean the entire movie is a deep dive into the psychological aspect of his mind- culminating in quite literally his monstrous self going on a rampage. As for what happens to Mary- she’s not in the Backrooms anymore as we see the mirror version of herself sitting in the room, meaning the Backrooms is remembering her.

I’m not saying you have to like a movie, but your criticism reads as if you weren’t even watching it to begin with.
  - (Spoilers) Was she really out? I thought that she and Phil were still inside.

Isn’t the Captain entity a replication of Clark, even though Clark is still inside?
    - I love how ambiguous it is at the end. They could be within the backrooms still, in some forward base within the backrooms or something. 
So good that you do not see a widow or any proof that she has escaped. 

Thematically we see her where she started: trapped in a small room with a man caught up in his own loop, pleading with her to see things his way, playing a therapist role. She tried to break free and ended up back where she stared.

Such a good film I liked it
      - I believe the implication is that she did get out, but she realizes Async is never going to let her go and alert the public so she's essentially a prisoner of Async
      - If you're familiar with his YouTube series that this is a continuation of, Mary is clearly brought through what is known as the "Threshold" which is the big doorway in the basement of Async labs in a large room with observation windows, this is in the real world which is also where the Async hallways etc are which are also shown to a degree in the YouTube series as well.

But it is the Backrooms after all and it could be interpreted that way sure, it's entirely possible, but the evidence doesn't really point that way. 
4. I think the movie would have done better not to show the monster. I do think the aesthetic of the movie is on point. The way the backrooms remembers things is very creative on how they portrayed that. Things half remembered, embedded in the rooms. It was great and really left me wanting to explore them more. I think it’s tough to inject a story line into something like this, but I understand needing a jumping off point. They are clearly gonna do a sequel and having a found footage scenario isn’t out of the question imo. Just like all other franchises, you need to set the table before you can rearrange the furniture. There is so much to explore.

## 3. I finally watched Eternal Sunshine

**Score:** 274
**Body:** I watched Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind last night and honestly, I wasn't expecting it to stick with me this much.

I went into it mostly knowing that it was supposed to be a really good movie, but I didn't expect the whole combination of romance, memory, and sci-fi to work as well as it did. It sounds like something that shouldn't fit together, but somehow it does. One thing I really loved was the way the movie jumps around through Joel's memories. The transitions between different moments felt so natural that I sometimes forgot I was watching memories disappearing in real time. It made the whole thing feel a lot more emotional than I expected.

And Jim Carrey was great. I'm so used to seeing him in comedies that watching him play Joel so quietly and seriously was kind of surprising. The music also deserves a lot of credit because it really added to the mood without feeling like it was trying too hard. By the time it ended, I was just sitting there thinking about it for a while. There's something about the idea of wanting to erase painful memories but still somehow holding onto the person connected to them that really got me.

What I don't understand is how this movie isn't talked about more. Maybe I'm just late to the party, but I feel like I should've watched this years ago.

## 5. Why is Digger so divisive?

**Score:** 138
**Body:** I’ve noticed a pretty big split in reactions to *Digger*. Some people talk about it like it’s a masterpiece, while others seem to really dislike it or find it hard to connect with.

I can honestly see both sides. There are elements I understand people loving, but I also get why others might strongly push back against it.

For those who have seen it, where do you land?

What do you think makes *Digger* great, and what do you think does not work about it?

I’m especially curious to hear from both sides: people who think it deserves the praise, and people who bounced off it completely.

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Let me ask this question: (spoilers)

>! Do you all think the reception of this movie would be much better if the whole play aspect was dropped and the story of Digger was presented straightforward like the trailers advertised? !<
  - The reception would be more positive but it would be a much less interesting film. 
  - spoilers:

Then it would be Don’t Look Up
 with Tom Cruise- ‘activism’ movies ring hollow in a world where income inequality is so stark and corruption so obvious. That’s why the cloying sincerity of Don’t Look Up got a lot of hate from audiences and critics.

I think Digger is satirizing/darkly depicting efforts at artistic ‘advocacy’ in our era. The play is chaotic and overdone and laying it on too thick- Tom Cruise’s critique. 
And then we learn that it’s ultimately a project of the wealthy, meant to give people some meaning and catharsis
. Meanwhile, in the real world- things are really getting worse. The air is bad, and climate change is threatening tom cruise’s child. Ultimately, we see that it’s the rich folks that have the power, and the dark, quasi-triumphant fantasy of digger and the president’s grisly deaths are revealed to be meaningless. 

We are pulled from the play in the movie (digger dies), to the movie setting, where we hear ‘level 4’ and watch people get up to leave into the dystopian future. Then finally we are pulled out of the movie itself as the we hear a loud final announcement, ‘Level 4’  that is meant to remind us that we, in real life, are like those people in the theater in the movie. I thought it was clever. For me it was a bleak depiction, and a grim call to action.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. The thing 'Arrival' overlooks about linguistics

**Score:** 321
**Body:** So, I don't know if this is a discussion that will interest anyone here, but as a linguist who somehow never got around to watching Arrival until now (and after years of people telling me, “What? How could you of all people never have watched Arrival??”), there was something about the movie – which I liked, by the way, and totally understand why people kept recommending it to me because how many big sci-fi movies have a linguist as the lead? – that kept nagging at me: its treatment of language.

This is clear in the scene where Louise is explaining to the crew the difficulty of establishing communication in order to ask the aliens what they really want to know: “What is your purpose here?” Louise explains why you can’t just translate that sentence word by word. Among other things, what does “your” refer to? They don’t want to know why “Joe Alien,” the particular alien standing in front of her, is there. They want to know why they are there. Why did all of them come to Earth? Why did all twelve ships land? So they first need to establish that distinction, and she’s absolutely right.

But watching the scene, my immediate thought was: this is also partly an English problem, because English doesn't grammatically encode distinctions of number in its second-person pronouns: you/your can refer to one person or several. Plenty of other languages grammatically distinguish things in their pronoun systems that English doesn't (number, gender, formality, inclusivity, etc.).

And that got me thinking about the actual premise of the movie. There aren't aliens only in Montana. There are twelve ships scattered around the planet, and multiple governments have teams trying to communicate with the same species, which means there should be linguists approaching Heptapod from completely different linguistic starting points.

To be fair to the movie, the different governments aren't running one giant, happy international research project. They're secretive about their progress, information is restricted, and eventually that cooperation starts breaking down. That's an important part of the plot. But there is some cooperation, particularly earlier on.

But it's weird how the linguistic side of that cooperation is almost completely absent from the plot. Because a problem that immediately occurs to Louise because she's working through English might not occur in exactly the same way to a linguist working through a language that already makes that distinction. And Louise didn’t “speak Alien,” but as a linguist, she would know that this particular challenge wasn't universal. Yet we never once see her advocate for the chance to speak directly with linguists working at the other sites who presumably had their own security clearance.

It’s like this possibility never crosses her mind at all. She seems perfectly content to work largely on her own, essentially from scratch. And this actually brings me to something even stranger: Louise herself seems to be the one and only linguist at the Montana site. (This is possibly the most important linguistic fieldwork project in human history, the military has assembled this enormous operation around it, and yet apparently the linguistics department consists of... Louise plus background extras staring at computer screens.)

So, there are rooms full of military personnel monitoring everything, scientists and technical staff everywhere, but when it comes to actually figuring out the language, everyone basically sits around waiting for this one linguist to do the work. Even if Louise were brought in as the lead linguist, wouldn't one of her first requests be: “I need other linguists”? Shouldn't the movie include a 20-second scene of her stating this need?

If, for whatever security and/or logistical reason, the US operation did not give her a linguistic team of her own, then surely the handful of people on Earth who could be most immediately useful to her would be the linguists doing exactly the same work at the other landing sites.

As a linguist, of course I’d love to watch a movie about different teams approaching the same unknown language with somewhat different sets of linguistic assumptions, but I get that this is not what Arrival was about, and that’s fine. My issue is that Louise is passionately and dutifully pursuing this goal, and yet she never even raises what seems to me like a pretty basic concern: other linguists around the world are trying to decipher the exact same language while approaching it through completely different linguistic systems.

Anyway, I guess we could frame all of this more broadly as a discussion about flaws in the script and the way it needs Louise to work in relative isolation for the story to function, but I'm mostly posting this because I'm curious if anyone else had a similar reaction and, as I've said, the topic of linguistics is particularly personal to me.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Anyone who sees their profession depicted in a film will most likely see that it bears very little resemblance to the real thing. But that's not a problem, because films are very rarely trying to depict reality. Instead they're using aspects of the profession (in this case a linguist) to tell the story that they want to tell. Any aspects of the real profession that don't help with the story, get ditched.

Arrival's ultimately a personal story of one woman. So a more realistic depiction of her working as part of a huge international team would change that story into something else entirely. It could be fantastic, but it would be totally different.

Basically trying to understand films by comparing how they measure up to reality is a losing game. It's just not what they're trying to do, 99% of the time. 
  - Nicely said.

I'm not sure the Indiana Jones movies would be improved by showing Indy repeatedly having grant applications denied and then spending six months slowly uncovering the Ark of the Covenant with a toothbrush.
    - I'm ready for the era of *Ultra Grounded Reimaginings*

And in every case, I think it was in an effort to make the film more enigmatic to just not answer all the questions.

“And anytime you have a film that's not neatly answering all the questions for the audience, you're opening yourself up to a lot of interpretation and analysis and people contemplating meanings. And one of those pieces was an essay on the uncanny written by Sigmund Freud.

“Stanley spent a lot of time reading that, thinking about it, talking about it. The essay essentially talked about Freud's theories about what elicits a feeling of uncanniness in a person. And the fact that the world of art specifically is best suited for creating a feeling of uncanniness.

“And that's, I think, because of a lot of the choices that Stanley made. And some of them are really kind of in the subconscious … subconsciously you feel it and it gives an uncanny feeling of somebody pulling the strings behind the scenes, like a greater force somehow. “And once people are aware that he was doing some kind of manipulation behind the scenes, that then opens them up to thinking that *everything* in the film was by design, which is *not* the case.
